title: Consolidated Fire Protection District of Los Angeles County
body:
The Consolidated Fire Protection District of Los Angeles County, run as the County of Los Angeles Fire Department and governed by the Board of Supervisors, provides fire protection and emergency medical service to the City of Santa Clarita and to all of the unincorporated valley.[1][2] The City is inside the district rather than a customer of it: the department lists Santa Clarita among the 47 cities whose service is paid for by a share of their property taxes and a voter-approved special tax, apart from the thirteen cities it bills under fee-for-service contracts.[1] Fifteen of its stations serve the valley, numbered 73, 76, 104, 107, 108, 111, 123, 124, 126, 128, 132, 143, 149, 150 and 156, from Newhall, Valencia, Canyon Country, Stevenson Ranch and Castaic; Station 126 on Citrus Street is the Battalion 6 headquarters, Station 150 on Golden Valley Road the Battalion 22 headquarters, and Station 76 in Valencia one of the County's three hazardous materials stations.[2][3] The newest permanent station, 104 on Golden Valley Road, was begun on August 9, 2018, to replace a temporary one.[4]

Before the district, the County's Department of Forester and Fire Warden guarded the valley.[5][1] Its Soledad Division office opened in Newhall in July 1923 with two paid men, and its headquarters station on San Fernando Road was built in the winter of 1928; in 1940 the division covered 1,014 square miles from the Santa Clara Divide to the Kern County line, answered 230 fires in 1939, and kept sixteen men at Newhall.[5] The same year the Soledad office opened, the Newhall Chamber of Commerce set out to form a fire district for the town: in May 1923 it named a committee to organize one, in September its chairman, P.C. Miller, reported that the Board of Supervisors had accepted the petition, and in October he reported that no money for apparatus would be available before the next March.[6][7][8] A Station 73 captain, Paul Peppard, wrote in 2014 that a Newhall Fire Protection District was formed in 1953 and shared the Newhall station with the forestry crews, engine 73 for the wildland and engine 273 for the town, until the two merged in 1954.[9] The County dates the Consolidated Fire Protection District to 1949, made from fire districts that had existed since the 1920s, and in 1992 the district annexed all the county's remaining unincorporated territory and took over the Forester and Fire Warden's duties.[1] Station 73 was dedicated in July 1958 beside the 1928 headquarters, which it replaced.[10] At the new City's first meeting, on December 15, 1987, the Council designated the County Fire Chief as City Fire Chief, and on June 23, 1988 it approved its service agreements with the County, the fire services contracts among them.[11][12]
footnotes: County of Los Angeles Fire Department, "History of the Consolidated Fire Protection District," https://fire.lacounty.gov/history/, read October 5, 2026: "In 1949, the Consolidated Fire Protection District was established by the Board of Supervisors through the consolidation of numerous fire districts which existed since the 1920s"; "In 1992, the CFPD annexed all the remaining unincorporated area in the County and unified the two departments into the CFPD"; under "Today's Service Area," "the CFPD serves all of the unincorporated area within Los Angeles County, as well as the following 60 incorporated cities," Santa Clarita among them; under "Property Tax Cities & Unincorporated Area," services "are funded primarily through a direct allocation of property taxes and a voter-approved special tax on all properties within the property tax cities served by the Fire District," the 47 cities listed including Santa Clarita; under "Fee-for-services Cities," "thirteen cities have entered into fee-for-service contracts with the CFPD," Santa Clarita not among them.

City of Santa Clarita, General Plan, Draft Safety Element, December 2021, pp. S-17, S-18 and S-25: "The Santa Clarita Valley is currently served by 15 LACFD fire stations: 73, 76, 104, 107 108, 111, 123, 124, 126, 128, 132, 143, 149, 150, and 156"; "As part of the Consolidated Fire Protection District, the City receives urban and wildland fire protection services from the LACFD"; "Station 76 is located in Valencia and serves the Santa Clarita Valley" as one of "three County fire stations that handle hazardous materials incidents."

County of Los Angeles, Location Directory, fire stations near Santa Clarita, https://locator.lacounty.gov/fire/Search?find=Fire+Stations&near=Santa+Clarita, read October 5, 2026, giving each station's address, "Station 126 (Battalion 6 Headquarters) ... 26320 Citrus St." and "Station 150 (Battalion 22 Headquarters) ... 19190 Golden Valley Road" among them.

"Groundbreaking: Fire Station 104, Golden Valley Road," SC1807, August 9, 2018, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sc1807.htm: "The new station, which replaces a temporary facility, will be located where Golden Valley Road becomes Newhall Ranch Road."

"History of L.A. County Dept. of Forester & Firewarden, Soledad Division," Newhall, February 27, 1940, submitted for the Newhall history compiled by Mary F. Brunner, Newhall Branch Librarian, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/library1040lacofire.htm: "The Soledad Office was first established July 1923, with two paid personnel"; "in the winter of 1928, the present station was constructed"; "The Soledad Division jurisdictional area consists of 1,014.07 square miles"; "The Soledad Division responded to 230 fires during 1939"; "Soledad Headquarters 16 personnel."

Newhall Chamber of Commerce, minutes of the board of directors, May 9, 1923, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/chamber1923-050923b.htm: "P.C. Miller, A.G. Thibaudeau, A.C. Swall and Fred R. Lamkin appointed to organize a Fire District and to look into the matter of securing a Fire House sight [sic]."

Newhall Chamber of Commerce, minutes, September 12, 1923, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/chamber1923-091223.htm: "P.C. Miller reported that the petition asking for the establishment of a fire district had been accepted by the County Board of Supervisors and that so far no protests had been offered."

Newhall Chamber of Commerce, minutes, October 31, 1923, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/chamber1923-103123.htm: "P.C. Miller reported that money would not be available, before next March, for purchasing fire apparatus."

Fire Capt. Paul Peppard, Fire Station 73-B, Battalion 6, Los Angeles County Fire Department, 2014, quoted on "Soledad Division Headquarters, County Forestry Dept.," FD2801, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/fd2801.htm: "Newhall Fire Protection District actually formed in 1953, so we technically had two different 'departments' operating out of one station: E73 for the wildland and E273 for the township"; "It wasn't until 1954 that the two 'departments' merged and became the Los Angeles County Fire Department."

"Dedication of Fire Station 73," FD5801, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/fd5801.htm: "Dedication of Fire Station 73 in Newhall (the building at right) in July 1958. It was built immediately north of the old (1928) Soledad Division Headquarters."

City of Santa Clarita, City Council minutes, December 15, 1987, item 24, Resolution No. 87-11, "appointing certain County officials to serve as City officials": "County Fire Chief designated as City Fire Chief."

City of Santa Clarita, City Council minutes, June 23, 1988, item 39, "Agreements for County Contract Services": "The City Attorney explained revisions that would be made to the Fire Services Contracts and stated that all other contracts are precisely as the County stated."

editorNotes.heading: The valley's stations
editorNotes.note: From the County's station directory, read October 5, 2026: 73, 24875 N. Railroad Avenue, Newhall; 76, 27223 Henry Mayo Drive, Valencia; 104, 26901 Golden Valley Road; 107, 18239 W. Soledad Canyon Road, Canyon Country; 108, 28799 Rock Canyon Drive; 111, 26829 Seco Canyon Road, Valencia; 123, 26321 N. Sand Canyon Road; 124, 25870 Hemingway Avenue, Stevenson Ranch; 126, 26320 Citrus Street (Battalion 6 headquarters); 128, 28450 Whites Canyon Road; 132, 29310 Sand Canyon Road; 143, 28580 Hasley Canyon Road, Castaic; 149, 31770 Ridge Route, Castaic; 150, 19190 Golden Valley Road (Battalion 22 headquarters); 156, 24505 Copper Hill Drive. The directory gives Santa Clarita as the city for those without a community named here.

editorNotes.heading: Contract or district
editorNotes.note: The City's own 2021 draft Safety Element says both that the City "contracts with the Los Angeles County Fire Department (LACFD) for fire services" and that "As part of the Consolidated Fire Protection District, the City receives urban and wildland fire protection services." The department's own lists settle it: Santa Clarita is a property-tax city of the district, not one of its thirteen fee-for-service contract cities.

relatedExisting: Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors #28275 (governs the district)
Daryl L. Osby, Los Angeles County Fire Chief 2011- (photograph) #4453
openQuestions: When did the Newhall and Saugus area, and the land that became the City, come into the Consolidated district? The County gives 1949 for the district and 1992 for the annexation of all remaining unincorporated territory, and Captain Peppard gives 1953 and 1954 for a Newhall district and its merger; no Board of Supervisors or LAFCO record of a Newhall or valley annexation was found (searched the legacy pages for "fire district", "fire protection district", "Newhall fire", "forester"; the web for "Newhall Fire Protection District" and the 1987 incorporation papers). LAFCO's district map gives "Established 06-22-83", which conflicts with 1949 and is not used.
Was the 1923 Newhall Chamber district ever formed? The minutes stop at October 1923 with no apparatus money before March 1924.
Title: the district's legal name, or "Los Angeles County Fire Department" with the district as an alias? Proposed: the legal name as title, the department's name as an alias.

dateFounded 1949 is the district's date from the County; the Forester and Fire Warden office goes back further (to the Forest Protection Act of 1905, per Captain Peppard, not otherwise verified). Should the record carry 1949?

title: County of Los Angeles Public Library
body:
The County of Los Angeles Public Library, the county's library system since 1912, serves the unincorporated valley from three branches: the Castaic Library on Sloan Canyon Road, opened in November 2008 and enlarged in March 2015; the Stevenson Ranch Library on The Old Road, which began as an express library in July 2011 and became a full library in March 2015; and the Acton Agua Dulce Library on Crown Valley Road in Acton, opened September 29, 2010 for Acton and Agua Dulce.[1][2][3][4] Before the Castaic branch, the outlying communities, Val Verde, Agua Dulce, Acton, Castaic and Friendly Valley among them, were served by the County's Santa Clarita bookmobile.[2][5] Inside the City of Santa Clarita the libraries have been the City's own since July 1, 2011.[6][7]

The County's library came to the valley on March 1, 1916, when a Newhall County Library opened in Robert and Christine Woodard's ice cream parlor, with Christine Woodard as its custodian at $5 a year; it moved into a small building of its own in 1923.[8][3] Its Newhall branch librarian in 1940, Mary F. Brunner, compiled the first comprehensive history of the valley.[9] A new Newhall branch at 22704 Ninth Street was dedicated on November 18, 1957, with Rose Buddell as branch librarian.[10] The second permanent branch, at 18536 Soledad Canyon Road in Canyon Country, opened on September 20, 1971, replacing the Saugus Mobilibrary that the County had run with the Saugus Union School District, and the Valencia Library was dedicated on May 24, 1972.[11][8] The City incorporated in 1987 with the three branches still the County's, and in April 1988 the Council agreed to the County Librarian's request to put City signs on them.[12] The City paid more than $5 million toward the County-operated Canyon Country Jo Anne Darcy Library at 18601 Soledad Canyon Road, which opened on November 17, 2001.[13] By 2010 the County served the valley with four libraries, at Canyon Country, Valencia, Newhall and Castaic, and a bookmobile, until the City withdrew its three from the County system on July 1, 2011.[5][6][7]
footnotes: LA County Library, "About Us," https://lacountylibrary.org/aboutus/, read October 5, 2026: "Founded in 1912, LA County Library is one of the largest and most innovative library systems in the US."

LA County Library, "Castaic Library," https://lacountylibrary.org/castaic-library/, read October 5, 2026: "27971 Sloan Canyon Rd, Castaic"; "The Castaic Library opened in November, 2008 in a 6,985 square foot storefront facility. To meet the needs of a growing community, a renovated and expanded library opened in March, 2015"; "Prior to the opening of the Castaic Library, the area was served by the Santa Clarita Bookmobile."

LA County Library, "Stevenson Ranch Library," https://lacountylibrary.org/stevenson-ranch-library/, read October 5, 2026: "25950 The Old Road, Stevenson Ranch"; "Library service in Stevenson Ranch began in July 2011 with the opening of Stevenson Ranch Express Library. In March, 2015, a new Stevenson Ranch Library opened to provide a full service library to the West Ranch communities. Library service in the Santa Clarita Valley area began in 1916 with the establishment of the original Newhall Library."

LA County Library, "Acton Agua Dulce Library," https://lacountylibrary.org/acton-agua-dulce-library/, read October 5, 2026: "33792 Crown Valley Rd, Acton"; a library "to serve the residents of the communities of Acton and Agua Dulce"; "The Library opened on September 29, 2010."

City of Santa Clarita, Vista Canyon Draft Environmental Impact Report, section 4.11, "Library Services," October 2010: "the County Library services the entire Santa Clarita Valley with four libraries and one bookmobile"; "The four libraries include the Canyon Country Jo Anne Darcy Library, Valencia Library, Newhall Library, and Castaic Library"; "A bookmobile service is provided to outlying areas of the Valley, such as Val Verde, Agua Dulce, Acton, Castaic, and the Friendly Valley Senior Community"; "Effective July 1, 2011, the City of Santa of Santa Clarita will assume operation of the three libraries within the City."

City of Santa Clarita, City Council minutes, August 24, 2010, item 15, Resolution No. 10-71, "to withdraw the City of Santa Clarita from the Los Angeles County Free Library System and assume the responsibility for the provision of library services within the City of Santa Clarita."

City of Santa Clarita, agenda report, "Santa Clarita Public Library Transition," January 9, 2018: "The Santa Clarita Public Library (SCPL) commenced operation as a City-provided service on July 1, 2011."

Leon Worden, "SCV Chronology: A Timeline of Historical Events," as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/timeline.htm: 1916, "March 1: Newhall County Library established inside Robert F. and Christine Woodard's ice cream parlor; Christine Woodard, custodian (librarian), salary: $5 per year"; 1923, "Newhall County Library moves into its own small building"; 1972, "May 24: Valencia Library dedicated."

"History of L.A. County Dept. of Forester & Firewarden, Soledad Division," 1940, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/library1040lacofire.htm: "The first comprehensive history of the Santa Clarita Valley was compiled in 1940 by Mary F. Brunner, the Newhall Branch Librarian."

"New Library Opens with Impressive Dedication Theme," The Newhall Signal and Saugus Enterprise, November 21, 1957, with "County Library Dedication 1957," AP0826, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/ap0826.htm: November 18, 1957, "Dedication of the Newhall Branch of the Los Angeles County Public Library in a new building at 22704 9th Street"; "Mrs. Rose Buddell, who has been the branch librarian for two years, was introduced as the permanent occupant of that job."

"Canyon Country Library Dedication," LB7101, September 20, 1971, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/lb7101.htm: "The Canyon Country Library at 18536 Soledad Canyon Road was the Los Angeles County Public Library system's second permanent library facility in the Santa Clarita Valley (following Newhall) when it opened September 20, 1971"; "it supplanted the Saugus Mobilibrary, which was a joint venture of the Saugus Union School District and the County Public Library."

City of Santa Clarita, City Council minutes, April 28, 1988, item 11, "City Signs on Library Buildings": "the request of the County Librarian to place City signs on each of the three county libraries"; approved on the motion of Boyer and Koontz.

"Jo Anne Darcy Library Grand Opening," SC0102, November 17, 2001, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sc0102.htm: "the city spearheaded construction and contributed more than $5 million toward a new, 17,000-square-foot, county-operated library building across the street at 18601 Soledad Canyon Road."

editorNotes.heading: Which library serves where
editorNotes.note: Read October 5, 2026: inside the City of Santa Clarita, the City's Santa Clarita Public Library (Canyon Country Jo Anne Darcy, Old Town Newhall, Valencia); in the unincorporated valley, the County's Castaic and Stevenson Ranch libraries, and for Agua Dulce the County's Acton Agua Dulce Library. The County's list of locations names no other branch in the valley.

relatedExisting: Jo Anne Darcy #16140 (the Canyon Country library is named for her)
Unveiling of Randy Wicks Memorial Wall at Valencia Library, 5-22-1997 (photograph) #4957
Arthur Buckingham Perkins #333 (at the 1957 Newhall dedication)
openQuestions: Title: the County's legal name "County of Los Angeles Public Library" (the City's 2010 resolution calls it the "Los Angeles County Free Library System"; the County now brands it "LA County Library"). Proposed: the legal name, the brand as an alias.
Is the Acton Agua Dulce Library inside the archive's valley? It sits in Acton but is the County's branch for Agua Dulce; the record names it for that reason.

The 1923 building and the 1916 founding rest on Leon Worden's chronology (the County's Stevenson Ranch page confirms 1916 only). Where the 1923 building stood, and the moves between, were not found in a contemporary source.
Mary F. Brunner has no person record; does she warrant one (librarian and compiler of the 1940 history)?

title: Santa Clarita Public Library
body:
The Santa Clarita Public Library is the City of Santa Clarita's library, with three branches: the Canyon Country Jo Anne Darcy Library, the Old Town Newhall Library and the Valencia Library.[1] It began on July 1, 2011, when the City took over the three County libraries inside its limits, and it has been run by City staff since July 1, 2018.[2][3] Under the state's Municipal Libraries Act it is managed by a Board of Library Trustees.[2] The unincorporated valley is served by the County's own branches at Castaic and Stevenson Ranch.[4][5]

The City Council voted on August 24, 2010, after a public hearing with 557 written comments and a petition, to withdraw from the Los Angeles County Free Library System and set up a municipal library, and in the same motion gave its management to a private firm, Library Systems & Services, LLC, under a contract through June 30, 2016; the vote was four to one, Bob Kellar against.[6] That October the Council created a citizens' advisory committee, appointing 37 members in November, and on July 12, 2011 adopted the library's first strategic plan.[7] The branches reopened as a City system over the Fourth of July weekend of 2011 with LSSI's employees as their staff, after two lawsuits against the change had been dismissed.[8][2] The City opened the Old Town Newhall Library on Lyons Avenue on September 29, 2012, replacing the 1957 County branch on Ninth Street, which had passed to the City in July 2011 and was closed.[9][10][11] On January 9, 2018 the Council voted unanimously to end the LSSI contract and staff the libraries with City employees from July 1, 2018, judging that the state's 2012 pension reform made that the cheaper course and estimating a first-year saving of $393,931; 54 LSSI employees then staffed the branches.[2][12][13]
footnotes: Santa Clarita Public Library, "About the Santa Clarita Public Library," https://library.santaclarita.gov/about/, read October 5, 2026: "On July 1, 2011, the City of Santa Clarita officially opened its doors to the Santa Clarita Public Library. Our library is comprised of three branches: Canyon Country Jo Anne Darcy, Old Town Newhall and Valencia"; "served over 440,000 patrons during the 2024-2025 fiscal year."

City of Santa Clarita, agenda report, "Santa Clarita Public Library Transition," City Council meeting of January 9, 2018, item 9: "The Santa Clarita Public Library (SCPL) commenced operation as a City-provided service on July 1, 2011"; "Since inception, SCPL has been operated and staffed through a contract with a private vendor, Library Systems & Services, LLC (LSSI), but in accordance with the Municipal Libraries Act (Education Code Section 18900 et seq.,) the SCPL is managed by the Library Board of Trustees"; "As a result of PEPRA, it is now cost effective to operate and staff SCPL with City employees"; "estimated first-year savings of $393,931"; "SCPL facilities and technology are already owned and administered by the City."

City of Santa Clarita, Vista Canyon Draft Environmental Impact Report, section 4.11, "Library Services," October 2010: "Effective July 1, 2011, the City of Santa of Santa Clarita will assume operation of the three libraries within the City."
LA County Library, "Castaic Library," https://lacountylibrary.org/castaic-library/, read October 5, 2026: "27971 Sloan Canyon Rd, Castaic."
LA County Library, "Stevenson Ranch Library," https://lacountylibrary.org/stevenson-ranch-library/, read October 5, 2026: "25950 The Old Road, Stevenson Ranch."

City of Santa Clarita, City Council minutes, August 24, 2010, item 15, "Withdraw from the County of Los Angeles Public Library System and Establishment of an Independent Municipal Library": "557 written comments and 1 petition were submitted on this item"; Resolution No. 10-71 "to withdraw the City of Santa Clarita from the Los Angeles County Free Library System and assume the responsibility for the provision of library services within the City of Santa Clarita"; "award a contract to Library Systems & Services, LLC for public library management services through June 30, 2016"; "Ayes: McLean, Ferry, Ender, Weste / Noes: Kellar."

"Santa Clarita Public Library Strategic Service Plan, 2011-2014," SC1102, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sc1102.htm: "On October 12, 2010, the City Council approved the creation of a Citizens Public Library Advisory Committee and on November 23, 2010, appointed thirty-seven people"; "The Santa Clarita City Council adopted its first Santa Clarita Public Library Strategic Service Plan July 12, 2011."

"Privatization and Pushback Proceed in Santa Clarita," American Libraries, July 27, 2011, https://americanlibrariesmagazine.org/2011/07/27/privatization-and-pushback-proceed-in-santa-clarita/: "opened its doors over the Fourth of July weekend as an independent city system"; "employees not of the city of Santa Clarita but of contract-services firm Library Systems and Services, Inc. (LSSI), whose five-year, $19-million contract"; "area residents filing two lawsuits, both of which were dismissed."

"City Library's First Chinese New Year Celebration," SC1204, January 23, 2012, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sc1204.htm: "the old Newhall Library building at 22704 9th Street. The city opened its big, new Old Town Newhall Library on Lyons Avenue September 29, 2012."

City of Santa Clarita, "Santa Clarita Public Library Annual Report, Fiscal Year 2012-2013," August 27, 2013, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/citylibraryannualreport082713.htm: "the grand opening of the Old Town Newhall Library, which more than 4,000 community members attended in September 2012."
"County Library Dedication 1957," AP0826, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/ap0826.htm: "the county library buiding (this building), which had become city property in July 2011, was closed."

City of Santa Clarita, City Council minutes, January 9, 2018, item 9, "Santa Clarita Public Library Transition": "Adopted Resolution Nos. 18-01 and 18-02; and BOLT Resolution No. 18-01. RESULT: APPROVED [UNANIMOUS]."

Stephen K. Peeples, "City Moves Toward Library Staffing Takeover by July 1," SCVNews.com, February 7, 2018, https://scvnews.com/city-moves-toward-library-staffing-takeover-by-july-1/: "Currently, 54 full-time LSSI employees staff the libraries"; "The private contractor has operated Santa Clarita's three libraries since 2011."

editorNotes.heading: Before 2011
editorNotes.note: The three branches it took over were the County's: Newhall from 1916, Canyon Country from 1971, Valencia from 1972. Their history is on the record for the County of Los Angeles Public Library.

openQuestions: Who sits as the Board of Library Trustees? The 2018 report and minutes show a Board of Library Trustees acting separately (BOLT Resolution No. 18-01) at the Council meeting, and Mayor Marsha McLean told American Libraries in 2011 that "Our library board of directors is the City Council," but no document read states the board's membership. Left out of the body beyond the report's own words.

A fourth branch: SCVNews (February 2018) quotes the City on a "Saugus Library and Arts Center, slated to open in 2021"; the library's own page in 2026 still lists three branches. Not found whether it was built; left out.
The Signal's articles on the 2010 and 2018 votes (signalscv.com) refused to load; the City's minutes and agenda report were used instead.
